newsitem.title: GERMANY: SOCCER-STOP MILKING THE GAME, KLINSMANN PLEADS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-STOP MILKING THE GAME, KLINSMANN PLEADS.

text.p: Germany captain Juergen Klinsmann has called on international soccer chiefs to stop what he called the "milking of football's cash cow" because it will destroy the quality of the game and the health of top players.

Klinsmann said the prospect of a European league, the continued expansion of international football and the huge money flooding into the game from television was leading to too many matches for top players.

"As long as the clubs make more money and the players earn more, there is no end to all this. UEFA or FIFA must stop this development. Or the players will say 'it can't go on'," he was quoted as saying by the German magazine Kicker on Thursday.

"The quality of the game must be paramount and not the continued milking of football's cash cow. It appears that all the financial possibilities must be taken advantage of -- to the cost of the top players. It is getting very difficult to get your body through all this."

Klinsmann, one of the highest earners at Bayern Munich, said there was no doubt that the planned expansion of the European Cup to include second-placed teams from major leagues would lead to a European league.
"It is getting more and more difficult for international players to play all the matches. Qualifying for European championships and World Cups is getting longer and longer, as are the tournaments.

"Now the European league is on its way because this event is no longer a Champions' League. Getting all the players to show solidarity about this is a long shot. But that is perhaps the best way to get the message across to FIFA."

"The quality is suffering. Look at the World Cup final in 1994. It kicked off at 12 noon (when temperatures were at their highest in the United States but television audience prospects were at their best). That has nothing to do with football."

Klinsmann said he also feared for the future of the game after the Bosman ruling, especially the future of young players. FIFA and UEFA also needed to act to stop major clubs buying up too many players to the detriment of their rivals.
"The first contract for an 18-year-old should be for four to five years at least, like in France, so that youth work is not destroyed," he said.

"UEFA and FIFA must also have a limit for the number of players a club can have on contract. Other than that, the big clubs will buy up all the market -- not to boost themselves but to weaken their rivals.
"The limit should be at 22 players. A limit for foreign players (in the Bundesliga) should be set at five or six."
